title: Quicksort: tracing and implementation
intro: Catch up on the key A Level ideas. Complete four retrieval questions, work through the examples, then practise and explain your reasoning.

questions.prompt: After partitioning [8,1,7,3,6] around pivot 6, where is the pivot?
Why does recursive quicksort need a base case?
questions.answer: To stop on empty or single-element partitions.
options: There is not enough information to determine the result.

To stop on empty AND single-element partitions.

questions.prompt: If the pivot finishes at index 3, give left and right recursive bounds in an array 0..6.
questions.answer: Left 0..2, right 4..6; do not include pivot index 3 again.
options: Left 1..2, right 4..6; do not include pivot index 3 again.
Left -1..2, right 4..6; do not include pivot index 3 again.
Left 0..2, right 4..6; do not include pivot index 3 again.
questions.feedback: Model answer: Left 0..2, right 4..6; do not include pivot index 3 again.

blocks.title: Key vocabulary
items: quicksort — Recursive sort using partitioning around a pivot.
partition index — Final index occupied by the pivot.
worst case — Input arrangement causing the most expensive run.
recursion stack — Storage used for nested calls.

blocks.title: Stop small subarrays
blocks.text: When low>=high there are zero or one elements to sort: return immediately.

blocks.title: Partition then divide
blocks.text: Partition places the pivot at its final index p. Do not recursively include index p.

blocks.title: Sort two sides independently
blocks.text: Call QuickSort on low..p−1 and p+1..high. The pivot itself stays fixed.
